title: Snakemake for biostatisticians
text:
Preface
Somewhere on your hard drive there is a folder with a paper in it, and in that folder there is a file called figure1.pdf.
Where did it come from? Which script made it? Was that script the current version of the script, or the one from before you fixed the bug in the data-generating function? If a reviewer asks you to change the sample sizes from 50, 100 and 400 to 50, 100, 400 and 1000, how many things do you have to remember to rerun, and in what order, before the number in the abstract is right again?
Most of us answer these questions with memory and discipline. Both work fine until the project gets big, or a coauthor touches it, or you come back to it after eight months. This tutorial is about answering them with a file instead.
A workflow manager is a program that you tell, once, which files depend on which other files and what command turns one into the other. After that it will build anything you ask for, run only what is actually out of date, and refuse to let a figure in your manuscript be older than the code that made it (unless you explicitly override it which isn’t easy to do). This tutorial focuses on one particular workflow manager: Snakemake.

title: Snakemake for biostatisticians
text:
Who this is for
Anyone who writes R, run simulations, and produce manuscripts or analysis reports. You should be comfortable in R. You do not need to know Python (Snakemake is written in Python, and its files are Python, but you will need about five minutes’ worth of it, all of which is explained), and you do not need to have used make or any other build tool.
Everything here runs on a laptop. However, one of Snakemake’s (many) party tricks is that the same workflow can be dispatched to a cluster rather easily, but that is out of scope here. See University of Iowa Biostatistics HPC tutorial.

title: Snakemake for biostatisticians
text:
What we build
One example runs through most of the book. It is a small simulation study of a problem you may have been asked about: what happens to confidence intervals when the model was chosen using the same data.
In this example we will: generate data, select variables by forward selection, and compare the intervals you get by naively refitting against the intervals you get by splitting the sample. Then we compute this over a grid of sample sizes and correlation levels, turn the results into a figure and a table, and compile the whole thing into a manuscript — so that changing one line of the simulation code and typing snakemake rebuilds the PDF, correctly, every time.
By the end the pipeline looks like this:





flowchart LR
  C[scripts/sim.R] --> S1[18 simulation<br/>result files]
  S1 --> F[out/figure1.pdf]
  S1 --> T[out/table1.tex]
  F --> P[build/paper.pdf]
  T --> P
  M[main.tex] --> P






8  A data analysis pipeline then applies the same ideas to a piece of applied collaborative work — raw CSV, cleaning, models, Table 1, rendered report — for readers whose focus is analysis rather than methods research (most of us). I focus on the manuscript pipeline here because it parallels where I learned to use Snakemake but the idea of 8  A data analysis pipeline is that the same ideas transfer.

title: Snakemake for biostatisticians
text:
Installing Snakemake
Snakemake is a Python package. Once you have a Python setup you like, install it there. E.g.:
python3 -m pip install snakemake
Check that it worked:
snakemake --version
This “book” was written against Snakemake 9.13. Version 8 introduced a number of changes to how cluster execution is configured, and a few flags used here do not exist in version 7 or earlier.
You will also want R with optparse and ggplot2; 7  Building a manuscript additionally uses tidyr, kableExtra and a LaTeX installation, and 8  A data analysis pipeline uses knitr and Quarto. Each example’s README.md lists what it needs.

title: Snakemake for biostatisticians
text:
Getting the examples
Every code block in this book is printed from a file in the examples/ directory of the tutorial repository, and every terminal transcript is pasted from a real run of that code. Nothing here is pseudocode. Clone the repository and follow along:
git clone https://github.com/lharris421/snakemake-tutorial.git
cd snakemake-tutorial/examples/01-first-rules
snakemake --cores 2

title: Snakemake for biostatisticians
text:
Acknowledgments and Scope
The format and spirit of this tutorial are modeled on the University of Iowa Biostatistics HPC tutorial by Patrick Breheny and Grant Brown, whose final chapter on Snakemake is the seed this grew from. The manuscript structure in 7  Building a manuscript follows the conventions in Patrick Breheny’s manuscript template and the general project workflow I’d suggest follows Iowa Biostat’s project workflow template.
This points to the fact that there are a number of great resources that already touch on using snakemake in practice. The goal of this tutorial is to help build a solid snakemake foundation rather than delve into all the intricacies.
I eventually plan to compile more complex examples of how to use snakemake… but I first need to decide which are generally useful.

title: 1  Running R from the command line
text:
1.1 Interactive work is not reproducible
Snakemake does not run R code. It runs commands, and it decides when to run them. So before any of it is useful, your analysis has to be something you can start from a terminal without clicking anything — and, ideally, something you can point at different parameter values without editing the file.
This chapter has nothing to do with Snakemake. If you already write scripts that take arguments and save their output to a file you name, skip to Chapter 2.
It is worth being blunt about this once, because everything else in the book follows from it.
Whatever is in your R session right now is the product of a history nobody has, including you. Objects created by code you have since edited or deleted. A package loaded by hand in March. A seed set before an experiment you abandoned. And if you saved the workspace on exit, all of that invisible state came back with you the next morning.
The practical consequence is that “it works” is not a claim you can check. A number in your session may or may not be what the current version of your code produces. There is no way to find out except to start a clean session and run the code from the top — which is exactly what running a script does.
None of this is an argument against working interactively. Interactive is how you figure out what the code should be; it is the right tool for exploring a dataset, staring at a model, and getting a plot to look right. The rule is narrower than that: nothing may exist only in your session. Once a piece of analysis is real, it belongs in a file that runs top to bottom, in a fresh session, and writes its output somewhere you named.
Snakemake is the machinery that makes the rule livable: it reruns from a clean session only the parts that are actually out of date, so insisting on scripts stops costing you the thing interactive work was buying.

title: 1  Running R from the command line
text:
TipDon’t save your workspace



Turn off the .RData prompt — in RStudio, Tools → Global Options → General, set “Save workspace to .RData on exit” to Never and clear “Restore .RData into workspace at startup”. Per project, the same two settings are SaveWorkspace: No and RestoreWorkspace: No in the .Rproj file; this repository’s has both.
It feels like losing something. What you lose is the illusion that your results survive a restart, and finding that out early is much cheaper than finding it out the week a paper is due.
crumbs: 1  Running R from the command line

title: 1  Running R from the command line
text:
1.2 Rscript
Rscript runs an R file top to bottom and exits:
Rscript sim.R
Two things change when your code runs this way rather than in RStudio.
The first is that the working directory is wherever your terminal is, not wherever the file is. If sim.R says readRDS("rds/thing.rds"), that path is resolved relative to the directory you were sitting in when you typed the command. Pick a convention and hold to it; the one used throughout this book is always run from the project root, so every path in every script is relative to the top of the project. Snakemake follows the same convention by default, which is convenient.
The second is that nothing prints unless you ask. Auto-printing at the top level is an interactive feature, so head(d) on its own line produces no output under Rscript; you need print(head(d)) or cat(). This matters more than it sounds like it should, because those prints become your log file in Chapter 6.
crumbs: 1  Running R from the command line

title: 1  Running R from the command line
text:
1.3 Taking arguments
A script that hard-codes n <- 100 can only ever do one thing. To run the same code at three sample sizes you would have to edit the file between runs, which is exactly the kind of manual step we are trying to eliminate. Instead, read the values from the command line.
The base R way is commandArgs(), which hands you the arguments as a character vector:


sim.R (excerpt)

args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
method <- args[1]
outfile <- args[2]

and is then called like this:
Rscript sim.R naive rds/sim-naive.rds
This is fine for two arguments. It gets bad quickly: the arguments are positional, so you have to remember the order, everything arrives as a character string that you have to convert yourself, and there is no way to give something a default.
crumbs: 1  Running R from the command line

title: 1  Running R from the command line
text:
1.4 optparse
The optparse package gives you named flags with types and defaults, which is what the rest of this book uses:


sim.R (excerpt)

library(optparse)

option_list <- list(
  make_option("--n", type = "integer", default = 100),
  make_option("--rho", type = "integer", default = 50),   # as a percent
  make_option("--method", type = "character", default = "naive"),
  make_option("--iterations", type = "integer", default = 200),
  make_option("--seed", type = "double", default = 1234),
  make_option("--out", type = "character", default = "rds/sim.rds")
)
opt <- parse_args(OptionParser(option_list = option_list))

Now the script is called with named arguments in any order:
Rscript sim.R --n 400 --rho 80 --method split --out rds/sim/n400_rho80_split.rds
and opt is a list: opt$n is an integer, opt$method is a string. Anything you leave off falls back to its default, so the script still runs as-is when you are poking at it interactively.






TipDefaults are documentation



Set the defaults to the values you use most often. Someone reading make_option("--iterations", type = "integer", default = 200) learns both what the flag is called and what a normal value looks like, and you get a script that runs unmodified when you source it by hand.

title: 1  Running R from the command line
text:
1.5 Output paths
The last convention: a script should write to a path it was told.


sim.R (excerpt)

dir.create(dirname(opt$out), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
saveRDS(res, opt$out)
cat("wrote", opt$out, "-- coverage:", round(mean(res$covered), 3), "\n")

Note the dir.create(). Snakemake creates the directories for a rule’s declared outputs before running it, but scripts that also work when you run them by hand shouldn’t count on that.
This is what makes a script composable. sim.R does not know it is part of a pipeline; it knows how to turn a set of parameters into output. The Snakefile in the next chapter is nothing more than a list of which parameters (or more generally, inputs) go with which outputs.

title: 1  Running R from the command line
text:
1.6 Where the results go
Two decisions that will save you pain later:
Results are files, and files should be named for what produced them. A file called n400_rho80_split.rds tells you the sample size, the correlation, and the method. A file called results2_final.rds tells you nothing.
Git is for source, not output. Commit the scripts and the inputs; let everything the code produces be rebuilt. That covers figures and tables as firmly as it covers a 200 MB .rds file — a figure is output no matter how small it is.
Computed results and finished products live in separate directories. Every example in this book writes serialized results — the expensive part — to rds/, and figures and tables to out/. Nothing is written anywhere else, and neither directory is tracked. It draws a clean line between the things that took an afternoon to compute and the things that can be redrawn in a second. Section 2.6 says more about the layout once you have seen a Snakefile.

title: 2  A first Snakefile
text:
2.1 Rules
Start in examples/01-first-rules. It contains two R scripts — sim.R, which runs the simulation for one method, and figure.R, which turns simulation output into a figure — and a file called Snakefile.
By hand, building the figure means running three commands in the right order:
That is not hard. It is just something you have to remember, and remember again every time you change one of the scripts, and remember correctly — because nothing stops you from rebuilding the figure without rerunning the simulation.
A Snakefile is a list of rules. A rule says: here are the files I need, here is the file I produce, and here is the command that gets from one to the other.
Read rule sim_naive as a sentence: to make rds/sim-naive.rds, given sim.R, run Rscript sim.R naive rds/sim-naive.rds.
A few mechanics:
Notice what is not here. Nothing about sim.R or figure.R is Snakemake-specific — figure.R ends in the ggsave() call you would have written anyway. Snakemake does not ask you to write your analysis differently; it asks you to say, in one file, which command turns which inputs into which outputs.

title: 2  A first Snakefile
text:
Snakefile

rule all:
    input:
        "out/figure1.pdf"

rule sim_naive:
    input:
        "sim.R"
    output:
        "rds/sim-naive.rds"
    shell:
        "Rscript sim.R naive {output}"

rule sim_split:
    input:
        "sim.R"
    output:
        "rds/sim-split.rds"
    shell:
        "Rscript sim.R split {output}"

rule figure:
    input:
        script = "figure.R",
        rds = ["rds/sim-naive.rds", "rds/sim-split.rds"]
    output:
        "out/figure1.pdf"
    shell:
        "Rscript {input.script} {output} {input.rds}"




{output} and {input} are substituted into the shell command. You write the filename once, in the output: block, and refer to it after that. This is not just brevity — it makes it impossible for the rule to declare one file and write a different one.
Inputs can be named, as in rule figure, where input.script and input.rds are referred to separately in the command. Without names, {input} expands to all of them, space-separated, in order.
Indentation matters, as in Python. Use four spaces and stay consistent.
sim.R is listed as an input, even though it is code rather than data. This is important. It is what makes “the script changed” a reason to rerun.

title: 2  A first Snakefile
text:
2.2 rule all
rule all is different. It has no output and no command — only inputs. It exists because of a rule Snakemake follows strictly:

Snakemake builds the first rule in the file, and whatever that rule needs.

So rule all is where you list the things you actually want to exist at the end. Everything else gets built because something in that list, directly or indirectly, depends on it. Anything not reachable from it is simply not part of a plain snakemake run — though you can still ask for it by name, which is the next section. By convention this is named rule all, but what matters is that it is first.

title: 2  A first Snakefile
text:
2.3 The dependency graph
From those four rules Snakemake works out the order for itself. Nothing in the file says the simulations come before the figure; it deduces that from the fact that rule figure needs files that rule sim_naive and rule sim_split produce.





flowchart LR
  sim_naive(sim_naive) --> figure(figure)
  sim_split(sim_split) --> figure
  figure --> allrule(all)






One node per rule, an arrow wherever one rule’s output is another’s input. This is a directed acyclic graph, the DAG, and it is what Snakemake works with rather than with your Snakefile directly. Two consequences worth internalizing early: anything with no path between the nodes can run at the same time (Chapter 6), and a cycle is an error rather than an infinite loop.
That picture is not hand-drawn — snakemake --rulegraph reports it, and Chapter 9 shows how to turn it into a file.

title: 2  A first Snakefile
text:
2.5 Building one thing
You can also name a target directly, which is invaluable when you are developing and want to check one piece:
snakemake --cores 1 rds/sim-naive.rds
Snakemake finds the rule that can produce that file, builds whatever it needs, and stops. You can also name a rule — snakemake --cores 1 figure — which asks for that rule’s outputs. The one restriction is that a rule whose output contains a wildcard cannot be named — Snakemake would have no way to know which values you meant:
$ snakemake --cores 1 sim
WorkflowError:
Target rules may not contain wildcards. Please specify concrete files or a rule
without wildcards at the command line …
So name the file instead, and the wildcards come from the filename as usual:
snakemake --cores 1 rds/200/sim/n50_rho0_naive.rds

title: 2  A first Snakefile
text:
2.6 One Snakefile, one project
Before going further, it is worth being explicit about what a “project” is here, because every example in this book is one and your own work should be too.
examples/01-first-rules is a complete, self-contained project. Copy that directory anywhere on your disk and everything still works — it has no dependency on the rest of this repository. The same is true of each of the other four. They are laid out side by side for convenience, but each is a miniature of a real repository: one paper, one analysis, one thing.
The layout that scales from these examples up to a real methods paper is:


the shape of a project

my-project/
  Snakefile          <- the map: every rule, in one file, at the root
  config.yaml        <- the settings (chapter 4)
  scripts/           <- the scripts the rules call
  R/                 <- functions the scripts share, one per file
  rds/               <- computed results
  out/               <- figures and tables

One Snakefile, at the root. Not one per subdirectory. The Snakefile is the only place that describes how the pieces of the project fit together, so a newcomer — a coauthor, a reviewer, you in a year — has exactly one file to open to find out what this project builds and what it builds it from. Snakemake does let you split rules across files with include:, and that is worth reaching for once a single file becomes genuinely unwieldy.
rds/ holds what the pipeline computes. Simulation output, fitted models, cleaned data — the objects that took time to produce and that everything else is derived from. I save results as .rds files, hence the name.
out/ holds what a human looks at. Figures and tables: the things that end up in the manuscript or the report.
The reason to split these rather than pile everything into one results/ folder is that the two halves behave completely differently. rds/ is expensive, is reused across a paper and a talk and a grant renewal, and may take days to regenerate — it is the thing worth backing up and worth sending to a coauthor. out/ is cheap: delete it and snakemake puts it back in seconds, from the contents of rds/. Once they are separate directories you can treat them differently, and Chapter 10 does exactly that: rds/ is the half you hand to a coauthor.
Neither rds/ nor out/ is tracked by git. Not because they are large, or binary, or likely to go stale — those are consequences, and reasoning from them means relitigating the question for every new kind of file. The rule is simpler than that:

Git is for source, not output.

Source is what a person wrote: the scripts, the Snakefile, the config, the .tex files. Everything in rds/ and out/ was produced by running that source, so none of it belongs in the repository.
Stated that way it also settles the case people otherwise talk themselves out of. A figure is small and it is genuinely convenient to look at a PDF on GitHub — but size has nothing to do with whether something is source, and out/figure1.pdf is as much an output as a four hundred megabyte .rds. If you want to see the figures, run snakemake. It takes seconds, and what you get is guaranteed to match the code you are looking at. My only exception is if the final paper / presenation on github serves as dissemination and is essentially fixed.
The one thing this costs you is that a fresh clone cannot show anybody a result until it has been rebuilt. When the rebuild takes days rather than seconds that is a real cost, and the answer is to share rds/ outside of git rather than to commit it — which is a topic of its own, and Chapter 10 is where it is dealt with.

text:
2.7 Try it

Add a line to rule all asking for out/nonexistent.pdf and run snakemake -n. Read the error carefully — you will see it again.
Ask for one simulation on its own: snakemake --cores 1 rds/sim-naive.rds. Then ask for it again.
Rename rule all to rule everything and check that a plain snakemake still does the same thing. Now move it to the bottom of the file and try again.

Chapter 2 ended with a working pipeline. What makes one worth having is not that it runs, but what it does the second time you ask — and, once a project is real, what it decides to leave alone.
Still in examples/01-first-rules, run it again:
This is the point of the exercise. Ask for the figure a hundred more times and you will get that message a hundred times. Now delete the figure and ask again:

title: 3  Rebuilding only what changed
section: 3.2 What counts as out of date
text:
3.2 What counts as out of date
Here is where Snakemake differs from make, and from most people’s expectations.
make asks one question: is the input newer than the output? If so, rebuild.
Snakemake asks two, and needs both answers to be yes. It keeps a record of every output it has ever made — in a directory called .snakemake/ — including a SHA-256 checksum of each input that went into it. A job is out of date when

an input’s timestamp is newer than the output’s, and
that input’s contents differ from what was recorded.

The timestamp is the gate and the checksum is the confirmation. So:
$ touch scripts/sim.R && snakemake -n
Nothing to be done (all requested files are present and up to date).
Touching a file does not trigger a rebuild, because the contents did not change. Change one character of sim.R, though, and everything downstream of it goes:
$ echo '## a real edit' >> scripts/sim.R && snakemake -n
Job stats:
job           count
----------  -------
all               1
figure1           1
manuscript        1
sim              18
table1            1
total            22
(That transcript comes from the larger example of Chapter 7, which is why there are 22 jobs rather than 4.)
Content is not the only trigger. Snakemake also stores the shell command used for each output, so editing a rule’s command — not just the script it calls — makes the affected outputs stale too.
Chapter 9 covers how to inspect and override all of this.

title: 3  Rebuilding only what changed
text:
3.3 Declare what a script sources
Scripts grow to the point where they share things — a set of functions, the labels and colors several figures use — and those live in files of their own, which is what R/ is for in Section 2.6 for shared functions. Snakemake has no way to know that a script reads another file unless you tell it, so a shared file has to be listed as an input to every rule whose script sources it. An undeclared dependency is the one failure mode Snakemake cannot warn you about: edit a shared function and every result built from it stays quietly stale.
That is also an argument for keeping such files narrow, because the declaration is all-or-nothing. In the larger example of Chapter 7 the simulation functions are in R/ and the plot labels and colors are in scripts/setup.R, listed separately: editing a hex code plans four jobs and leaves the simulations alone, while editing a function plans all twenty-two. Had both lived in one file, the color change would have rerun eighteen simulations, because Snakemake cannot tell which half of a file you touched.

title: 3  Rebuilding only what changed
text:
3.4 Try it

Delete out/ and rebuild. Time it. Then delete rds/ as well and compare.
Change the n <- 100 line in sim.R to n <- 200 and run snakemake -n. Which jobs are planned, and why?
Change a comment in figure.R, then run snakemake -n. Does the simulation rerun? Should it?

title: 4  One rule, many jobs
text:
4.1 A wildcard is a blank space in a filename
Look again at the Snakefile from Chapter 2 and notice how much of it is copied and pasted:
Two rules, identical but for the word naive versus split. Now imagine the real version of this simulation: three sample sizes, three correlation levels, two methods. Eighteen rules, all the same, and one typo away from a figure that silently mixes up two scenarios.
Wildcards fix this. Move to examples/02-wildcards.
The output is no longer a filename; it is a pattern. The parts in braces are wildcards, and they work backwards: when something asks for rds/sim/n400_rho80_split.rds, Snakemake matches that name against the pattern, concludes that n is 400, rho is 80 and method is split, and substitutes those values into the command wherever {wildcards.…} appears.
This is the mental adjustment that makes Snakemake click. You do not tell it to run the simulation eighteen times. You tell it what a result file is called as a function of its parameters, and then you ask for the files you want.

title: 4  One rule, many jobs
text:
Snakefile (excerpt)

rule sim:
    input:
        "sim.R"
    output:
        "rds/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.rds"
    shell:
        "Rscript sim.R "
        "--n {wildcards.n} "
        "--rho {wildcards.rho} "
        "--method {wildcards.method} "
        "--out {output}"

title: 4  One rule, many jobs
text:
4.2 wildcard_constraints






ImportantWildcards match anything, including nonsense



A wildcard is a regular expression, .+ by default. Nothing in the rule above says method has to be naive or split, so asking for rds/sim/n50_rho0_bayes.rds produces a perfectly valid job that runs sim.R --method bayes and fails inside R.


Constraints fix that:


Snakefile (excerpt)

wildcard_constraints:
    iterations = r"\d+",
    n = r"\d+",
    rho = r"\d+",
    method = "[a-z]+"

r"\d+" is a regular expression matching one or more digits; the r prefix marks a raw string, so the backslash reaches the regex intact. Declared at the top level they apply to every rule, and they can also be attached to a single rule, as Chapter 7 does.
Two reasons to bother:
Ambiguity. With unconstrained wildcards there is more than one way to match n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.rds against a name containing extra underscores, and Snakemake resolves it by its rules rather than yours.
Failing early. Without the \d+ on {n}, asking for rds/200/sim/nfifty_rho0_naive.rds matches quite happily —
wildcards: iterations=200, n=fifty, rho=0, method=naive
— and Snakemake goes off and runs sim.R --n fifty, which dies inside R however long the job takes to get that far. With the constraint, nothing can produce that file and you are told so before anything starts.

title: 4  One rule, many jobs
text:
4.3 Naming files so this works
Wildcards make your file-naming scheme part of the pipeline’s logic, which is worth two minutes of thought up front:

Put every parameter that changes into the name. If two runs differ in anything, their outputs must differ in name, or one will overwrite the other and Snakemake will believe both are up to date.
Use a separator that cannot appear in a value. These examples use _ between fields and stick to digits and lowercase letters within a field.

The scheme here is n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.rds, with rho as a percentage so that it stays an integer — rho50 rather than rho0.5, because a decimal point in a filename is an invitation to trouble.

title: 4  One rule, many jobs
text:
4.4 expand()
Something still has to say which eighteen files we want. That is expand() in the figure rule (what actually needs to results):


Snakefile (excerpt)

rule figure:
    input:
        script = "figure.R",
        rds = expand("rds/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.rds",
                     n = [50, 100, 400],
                     rho = [0, 50, 80],
                     method = ["naive", "split"])
    output:
        "out/figure1.pdf"
    shell:
        "Rscript {input.script} {output} {input.rds}"

expand() takes a pattern and some lists and returns every combination of them, so that one call returns a list of 3 × 3 × 2 = 18 filenames. Those are the inputs of rule figure, which is what causes all eighteen simulations to run.






NoteThe Python you need



[50, 100, 400] is a list, the same idea as c(50, 100, 400) in R, and n = [50, 100, 400] passes it to expand() by name. That is essentially the entire Python vocabulary required to use Snakemake: lists, strings in quotes, and the occasional dictionary in Chapter 5 (and even that is optional).


The grid is written out inside the rule that needs it, rather than in variables at the top of the file, and that is usually where it belongs: another rule is free to sweep a different one, and a supplementary figure covering only the large sample sizes would simply expand over fewer. When several rules genuinely share a grid, define it once above them.
The script on the other end receives all eighteen filenames as arguments and stacks them:


figure.R (excerpt)

args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
outfile <- args[1]
infiles <- args[-1]

res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(infiles, readRDS))

Note that expand() fills wildcards in, and {wildcards.n} reads them back out. These are opposite operations, and it is worth being clear about which one you are doing: expand() appears in the rule that consumes many files, and {wildcards.…} in the rule that produces them.

title: 4  One rule, many jobs
section: 4.6 Building one cell of the grid
text:
4.6 Building one cell of the grid
Because the output is a pattern, you can ask for any file it can match, whether or not anything else wants it:
$ snakemake --cores 1 rds/sim/n50_rho0_naive.rds
Using shell: /bin/bash
Provided cores: 1 (use --cores to define parallelism)
Rules claiming more threads will be scaled down.
Job stats:
job      count
-----  -------
sim          1
total        1

Select jobs to execute...
Execute 1 jobs...

localrule sim:
    input: sim.R
    output: rds/sim/n50_rho0_naive.rds
    jobid: 0
    reason: Missing output files: rds/sim/n50_rho0_naive.rds
    wildcards: n=50, rho=0, method=naive
    resources: tmpdir=/var/folders/gz/hbrw64n97wb0vy5prhnxst400000gp/T
wrote rds/sim/n50_rho0_naive.rds -- coverage: 0.823 

Finished jobid: 0 (Rule: sim)
1 of 1 steps (100%) done
This is how you develop. Rather than running the whole grid to find out whether your new method works, ask for one small scenario, look at it, and only then let the rest go.
This is also extremely powerful, because now if you want a certain simulation… you just have to ask for it rather than edit an R file and run it.

text:
4.7 Try it

title: 5  Configuration
text:
5.1 config.yaml
sim.R in Chapter 4 has 200 iterations written into it, which is the wrong place: you will want 20 while you are debugging and 1000 for the final results, and changing that should not mean editing the simulation code.
Move to examples/03-config, which puts shared parameters into a single file.
YAML is about as simple as it looks: key: value, one per line, lists in square brackets, # for comments. Load it at the top of the Snakefile:
and everything in it is available as config, a dictionary: config["iterations"] is 200. Use config.get("key", default) when a setting is optional.
Notice how little is in there. A config is for settings that apply to the project as a whole — iterations means the same thing to every simulation.

title: 5  Configuration
text:
config.yaml

# Settings that apply to the whole project.  Drop `iterations` to 20 for a fast
# run that checks the plumbing; put it back to 200 for results you would show
# anyone.
iterations: 200




Snakefile (excerpt)

configfile: "config.yaml"

title: 5  Configuration
section: 5.2 Runs that don’t overwrite each other
text:
5.2 Runs that don’t overwrite each other
This one setting is treated differently, and it is the most useful idea in this chapter. iterations is not passed to the script and forgotten — it names the directory the results go in:


Snakefile (excerpt)

## The iteration count names the directory the results go in, so a 20-iteration
## smoke run and a 1000-iteration final run sit side by side instead of
## overwriting each other.  ITER picks which of them the figure is built from.
ITER = config["iterations"]



Snakefile (excerpt)

rule sim:
    input:
        script = "scripts/sim.R",
        functions = glob.glob("R/*.R")
    output:
        "rds/{iterations}/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.rds"
    shell:
        "Rscript {input.script} "
        "--n {wildcards.n} "
        "--rho {wildcards.rho} "
        "--method {wildcards.method} "
        "--iterations {wildcards.iterations} "
        "--out {output}"

{ITER} never appears in that rule: the count arrives as the wildcard {wildcards.iterations}, read back out of the filename that was asked for by rule figure, just like {wildcards.n}.
The figure rule collects the set ITER points at:


Snakefile (excerpt)

        rds = expand("rds/{iterations}/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.rds",
                     iterations = ITER,
                     n = [50, 100, 400],
                     rho = [0, 50, 80],
                     method = ["naive", "split"])

title: 5  Configuration
text:
5.3 Overriding from the command line
Any config value can be replaced for a single run with --config:
snakemake --cores 4 --config iterations=20
which is the fastest way to check that a pipeline is wired up before committing to the real thing:
$ snakemake --cores 4 --config iterations=20

real    0m3.527s
user    0m4.771s
sys 0m0.612s
$ snakemake --cores 4

real    0m9.605s
user    0m27.178s
sys 0m0.775s
Five seconds against eleven, for a grid that would take considerably longer at the iteration counts of a real paper.

title: 5  Configuration
text:
5.4 Try it

Run with --config iterations=20, then again with --config iterations=200. What does Snakemake rerun, and why?
Delete the wildcard_constraints block and ask for rds/sim/n50_rho0_na_ive.rds. What happens, and what did {method} match?

title: 6  Parallelism, logs and benchmarks
text:
6.1 –cores
Once your work is expressed as a DAG, you get the parallelism for free — Snakemake already knows which jobs do not depend on each other.
With eighteen independent simulations and four cores, four run, and as each finishes another starts, until all eighteen are done and the figure can go. There is nothing to configure — the ordering falls out of the DAG.
--cores all uses every core you have. On a laptop you are also using for other things, leave one or two free; on a shared server, be a good citizen and pick a reasonable number.

title: 6  Parallelism, logs and benchmarks
text:
snakemake --cores 4








NoteTwo kinds of parallel



--cores controls how many jobs run at once, and that is usually the only kind of parallelism you need for a simulation study. It is unrelated to parallelism inside a job (mclapply, future, a multithreaded BLAS). If a rule does use threads internally, tell Snakemake with threads: so its accounting stays honest:
rule sim:
    threads: 4
    shell: "Rscript sim.R --cores {threads} ..."
Then --cores 8 runs two such jobs at a time rather than eight.
Sometimes if each iteration is very expensive, you may want to parallelize over iterations. This sort of mechanism can be found in University of Iowa Biostatistics HPC tutorial.

title: 6  Parallelism, logs and benchmarks
text:
6.2 Logs
Once eighteen jobs are interleaving their output, the terminal becomes unreadable, and the run you actually want to is buried. The log: directive gives each job its own file:


Snakefile (excerpt)

rule sim:
    input:
        script = "scripts/sim.R",
        functions = glob.glob("R/*.R")
    output:
        "rds/{iterations}/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.rds"
    log:
        "logs/{iterations}/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.log"
    benchmark:
        "benchmarks/{iterations}/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.tsv"
    shell:
        "Rscript {input.script} "
        "--n {wildcards.n} "
        "--rho {wildcards.rho} "
        "--method {wildcards.method} "
        "--iterations {wildcards.iterations} "
        "--out {output} > {log} 2>&1"

Two details. The log file is declared by log: but nothing writes to it automatically — the redirection > {log} 2>&1 at the end of the shell command is what does it (2>&1 catches errors as well as normal output). And the log path carries the same wildcards as the output, so each job gets its own file rather than eighteen jobs overwriting one.
Anything the script prints lands there:
$ cat logs/200/sim/n400_rho80_naive.log
wrote rds/200/sim/n400_rho80_naive.rds -- coverage: 0.78 
Which is worth designing for. A script that prints its parameters, its sample size after exclusions, and a summary of what it computed gives you a log directory that answers most questions without rerunning anything. Chapter 8 leans on this heavily.
Logs also survive failure. When a job dies, Snakemake tells you which log to read, and the R error message is sitting in it — as opposed to being lost in the scrollback of a parallel run.






ImportantSnakemake will not delete a log file



Outputs of a failed job are removed so that a half-written file is never mistaken for a real one. Logs are deliberately kept, because they are the evidence. This also means a log from a run sticks around until the job runs again.

title: 6  Parallelism, logs and benchmarks
text:
6.3 Benchmarks
benchmark: records how long a job took:
rule sim:
    benchmark: "benchmarks/sim/n{n}_rho{rho}_{method}.tsv"
$ cat benchmarks/200/sim/n400_rho80_naive.tsv
s   h:m:s   max_rss max_vms max_uss max_pss io_in   io_out  mean_load   cpu_time
1.67    0:00:01 0   0   0   0   0.00    0.00    61.38   0
The first column is seconds. This is how you find out that one corner of your parameter grid takes forty times as long as the rest, which is worth knowing before you scale the whole grid up by a factor of ten.

title: 6  Parallelism, logs and benchmarks
text:
6.4 Interrupting and resuming
Snakemake is designed to handle being stopped.
Terminating processes on user request, this might take some time.
What survives is everything that had already finished. Those outputs stay on disk, and the next run does not rebuild them; it starts from wherever the interruption left the pipeline. So the cost of stopping a twelve-hour run after four hours is only the handful of jobs that were in flight at that moment.
The jobs that were in flight need one more thought, because a killed job may have got as far as writing part of its output. Snakemake tracks that, and rather than letting a truncated file pass for a real result it stops the next run:
IncompleteFilesException:
The files below seem to be incomplete. …
Incomplete files:
rds/200/sim/n400_rho80_split.rds
The fix is to say so explicitly:
snakemake --cores 4 --rerun-incomplete
which discards the suspect files and rebuilds them.

title: 6  Parallelism, logs and benchmarks
text:
6.5 Try it

In examples/03-config, run with --cores 1, then --cores 4, and compare. Why is the speedup less than four?
Add a log: directive to the figure rule in examples/03-config and check that ggsave’s message ends up in it.

title: 7  Building a manuscript
text:
7.1 The rule
Move to examples/04-manuscript. It is the simulation study of the last three chapters with two things added: rules that turn the eighteen result files into a figure and a table, and a rule that compiles a paper out of them.
Here is the situation this chapter is about. You are using an editor that rebuilds your PDF every time you save, so the document always matches its LaTeX source. It does not match its figures: out/figure1.pdf was made by some script at some point, and if you change the simulation nothing tells the manuscript about it. The document is only as current as the last time you remembered to rerun things.
Making the manuscript a rule closes that gap.
latexmk is doing the LaTeX-specific work — running pdflatex and BibTeX as many times as it takes for references and citations to settle. Snakemake’s contribution is the input: block: the PDF depends on the figure and the table, which depend on the simulations, which depend on the code. One command now walks the entire chain.
Written out, the rules make this shape:
flowchart LR
  sim(sim) --> figure1(figure1)
  sim --> table1(table1)
  figure1 --> manuscript(manuscript)
  table1 --> manuscript
  manuscript --> allrule(all)
Every arrow is a line in the Snakefile, and every one of them is a claim that Snakemake will enforce. Nothing reaches build/paper.pdf except through a rule.
That diagram is not hand-drawn: it is the graph Snakemake reports for this workflow, and you can get one for your own with
One node per rule, which is the readable view. snakemake --dag draws one node per job instead, so sim becomes the eighteen separate boxes it really is (Chapter 9).
paper.tex itself is only a wrapper — a document class, \input{preamble.tex}, and \input{main.tex} — so that the prose lives in one file and the formatting in another:

title: 7  Building a manuscript
text:
Snakefile (excerpt)

## The manuscript depends on the figure and the table, which depend on the
## simulations, which depend on the code.  That chain is the whole point: change
## sim.R and `snakemake` rebuilds the PDF, through every step in between.
rule manuscript:
    input:
        tex = "paper.tex",
        shared = ["main.tex", "preamble.tex"],
        config = "config.yaml",
        figure = "out/figure1.pdf",
        table = "out/table1.tex"
    output:
        "build/paper.pdf"
    log:
        "logs/paper-latexmk.log"
    shell:
        "latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode -outdir=build {input.tex} "
        "> {log} 2>&1"






snakemake --rulegraph | dot -Tpdf > rules.pdf




paper.tex

%% Layout wrapper: document class, preamble, and the content.  All of the actual
%% writing is in main.tex, so that changing the formatting never means touching
%% prose -- and a second version of the paper is a second wrapper, not a copy.
\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\input{preamble.tex}

\begin{document}
\maketitle
\input{main.tex}
\end{document}







NoteJournal versions, arXiv, supplements



A real paper is eventually built more than one way. The separation above is what makes multiple versions with different formats lightweight — each variant is another wrapper around the same main.tex, and another rule producing its own PDF.
Setting that up well is a LaTeX question rather than a Snakemake one, and pbreheny/manuscript-template already covers it.

title: 7  Building a manuscript
text:
7.2 The cascade
This is the payoff, so it is worth watching happen. Everything is currently built and up to date. Now change one line in the simulation code:
$ echo '## a real edit' >> scripts/sim.R && snakemake -n
Job stats:
job           count
----------  -------
all               1
figure1           1
manuscript        1
sim              18
table1            1
total            22
Twenty-two jobs: eighteen simulations, the figure, the table and the PDF. In the right order, with no decisions from you, and — the part that matters — with no possibility of a version of the paper containing a figure from before the change (provided you’ve specified the Snakefile completely).
Compare the alternative, which is remembering to run four things in order and being right about it every time, for the entire life of the project (and with the number being much greater than four as the manuscript grows).






WarningLaTeX’s own idea of what is up to date



latexmk does its own dependency tracking and will sometimes decide there is nothing to do even when Snakemake has just asked it to rebuild. If a rerun leaves the PDF unchanged when you expected otherwise, delete the build/ directory and try again.

7.3 Try it

Change the figure’s y-axis label and run snakemake --cores 4. Which jobs run? Which do not, and why not?

title: 8  A data analysis pipeline
text:
8.1 The pipeline
Many biostatisticians spend more time on analyses than on simulation studies, and the shape of the work is different: instead of a fan-out over a parameter grid, a mostly linear chain from a file someone emailed you to a report you send back. The Snakemake ideas transfer directly..
Move to examples/05-analysis. It is a small randomized trial: 200 participants, two arms, FEV1 measured at baseline and week 12.
flowchart LR
  clean(clean) --> table1(table1)
  clean --> analysis(analysis)
  clean --> figure1(figure1)
  clean --> report(report)
  analysis --> table2(table2)
  table1 --> report
  table2 --> report
  figure1 --> report
  report --> allrule(all)
clean feeds nearly everything, because every product describes the same analysis set. table1 says who was studied and table2 what happened to them, which is why one hangs off the cleaned data and the other off the models.

title: 8  A data analysis pipeline
text:
$ snakemake --cores 4
Job stats:
job         count
--------  -------
all             1
analysis        1
clean           1
figure1         1
report          1
table1          1
table2          1
total           7

title: 8  A data analysis pipeline
text:
8.2 Cleaning once


scripts/clean.R (excerpt)

raw <- read.csv(opt$infile, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
log_step <- function(d, msg) {
  cat(sprintf("%-45s n = %d\n", msg, nrow(d)))
  invisible(d)
}
log_step(raw, "raw file")

d <- raw[!duplicated(raw$patient_id), ]
log_step(d, "after dropping duplicate patient records")

## Sex arrives as F/f/female/Female/M/male/Male
d$sex <- ifelse(toupper(substr(d$sex, 1, 1)) == "F", "Female", "Male")

## Ages over 120 are data entry errors, not centenarians
d$age[d$age > 120] <- NA
log_step(d[!is.na(d$age), ], "with a usable age")

d$visit_date <- as.Date(d$visit_date, format = "%m/%d/%Y")
d$arm <- factor(d$arm, levels = arm_levels)
d$smoker <- factor(d$smoker, levels = c("Never", "Former", "Current"))
d$change <- d$fev1_wk12 - d$fev1_base

## The primary analysis needs a week 12 measurement
d <- d[!is.na(d$change), ]
log_step(d, "with a week 12 measurement (analysis set)")

Every decision about the data is in this one script, and it announces each one:
$ cat logs/clean.log
raw file                                      n = 201
after dropping duplicate patient records      n = 200
with a usable age                             n = 199
with a week 12 measurement (analysis set)     n = 191
wrote rds/clean.rds 
That is the participant flow for your CONSORT diagram, produced as a side effect of the pipeline rather than counted by hand, and regenerated every time the data changes. When the coordinator sends an updated export in June, snakemake reruns everything downstream and this log tells you immediately whether the exclusions still look the way they did in March.
The alternative — each analysis script starting with its own read.csv() and its own quiet decisions about who to drop — is how two tables in the same report end up with different denominators.

title: 8  A data analysis pipeline
section: 8.3 The report is a view, not a computation
text:
8.3 The report is a view, not a computation
Here is the part specific to analysis work. It is normal to put everything in one .qmd file: read the data, fit the models, print the tables, write the text. It works, and it has two failure modes that get worse as the project grows.
The first is time. A report that refits everything takes as long as the slowest model every time you fix a typo, and the temptation is to start caching chunks, which I’ve had very little luck with.
The second is scope. Rendering becomes all-or-nothing — you cannot ask for just the models — and the results exist only inside the rendered HTML, so the next project that needs them starts by copying and pasting.
Splitting it fixes both. The scripts compute and save; the report reads and displays:


report.qmd (excerpt)

```{r}
#| include: false
library(knitr)
d <- readRDS("rds/clean.rds")
tab1 <- readRDS("rds/table1.rds")
tab2 <- readRDS("rds/table2.rds")
```

The report does no computing of its own. It reads the objects the pipeline
produced and displays them, so that rendering it can never quietly change a
result.



Snakefile (excerpt)

## Listing every object the report reads is what makes the report trustworthy:
## it cannot be rendered against a stale table or a figure from last month.
rule report:
    input:
        qmd = "report.qmd",
        clean = "rds/clean.rds",
        table1 = "rds/table1.rds",
        table2 = "rds/table2.rds",
        figure1 = "out/figure1.png"
    output:
        "report.html"
    log:
        "logs/report.log"
    shell:
        "quarto render {input.qmd} --to html > {log} 2>&1"

Listing each object the report reads is what makes the report trustworthy. Rendering it cannot use a stale table, because Snakemake will rebuild the table first. And the fitted models are in rds/analysis.rds, so the manuscript you write next year can load them without rerunning anything.
Everything the report needs to say in prose comes through inline R:


report.qmd (excerpt)

The estimated treatment effect is `r attr(tab2, "headline")` L in the adjusted
model, and is insensitive to which covariates are included.

so the sentence and the table cannot disagree.

8.5 When the data changes
Which it will, usually the week after you send the report. Drop in the new data and:
snakemake --cores 4
Cleaning reruns, the models refit, Table 1 and the figure regenerate, the report re-renders, and the participant-flow log tells you what changed about the analysis set. The work of a data update goes from an afternoon of retracing your steps to one command and a careful look at one log file.

title: 9  When things go wrong
text:
9.1 Look before you run
Most of the trouble people have with Snakemake comes from one of two questions: why is it doing that? and why is it not doing that? This chapter provides some useful tools for debugging.
-n is the answer to a surprising fraction of problems. It builds the DAG, decides what it would do, and does none of it:
Each planned job comes with a reason: line:

text:
snakemake -n              # what would you do?

title: 9  When things go wrong
section: 9.2 What is the status of each file?
text:
9.2 What is the status of each file?
--summary lets you inspect the files statuses, one row per file Snakemake knows about:
$ snakemake --summary | head -6
output_file date    rule    log-file(s) status  plan
build/paper.pdf Thu Aug  6 08:26:37 2026    manuscript  logs/paper-latexmk.log  ok  no update
out/figure1.pdf Thu Aug  6 08:26:37 2026    figure1 logs/figure1.log    ok  no update
rds/200/sim/n50_rho0_naive.rds  Thu Aug  6 08:26:35 2026    sim logs/200/sim/n50_rho0_naive.log ok  no update
rds/200/sim/n50_rho0_split.rds  Thu Aug  6 08:26:35 2026    sim logs/200/sim/n50_rho0_split.log ok  no update
rds/200/sim/n50_rho50_naive.rds Thu Aug  6 08:26:35 2026    sim logs/200/sim/n50_rho50_naive.log    ok  no update
The plan column tells you what would happen and the status column whether the recorded provenance still matches.

title: 9  When things go wrong
text:
9.3 Making it rerun anyway







Command
What it does




snakemake -R sim
rerun rule sim and everything downstream


snakemake --forcerun sim
same thing, spelled out


snakemake -f out/figure1.pdf
rebuild just that file


snakemake -F
force everything, from scratch


snakemake --delete-all-output
delete everything the workflow produced



-R is what you can use when you say “I changed something Snakemake cannot see”. E.g. a package upgrade (more on this in the future).

title: 9  When things go wrong
text:
9.4 Making it not rerun
The mirror image: files are current but Snakemake wants to rebuild them, usually because they were copied from somewhere or restored from a backup.
snakemake --touch
--touch marks every output as up to date without running anything. Use it when you know the files are fine, and note that you are making an assertion Snakemake cannot check.
The case where you will actually want it is results that arrived from a collaborator without the metadata that explains them (.snakefile), and there --touch on its own is not enough — Chapter 10 has the recipe.
--rerun-triggers narrows what Snakemake is allowed to notice. All five signals are on by default:
snakemake --rerun-triggers code input mtime params software-env   # the default
snakemake --rerun-triggers input                                  # only file contents
which is occasionally useful.
[to be continued…]

title: 9  When things go wrong
text:
9.5 The errors you will see

9.5.1 No rule to produce
$ snakemake --cores 1 out/coverage-summary.csv
MissingRuleException:
No rule to produce out/coverage-summary.csv (if you use input functions make sure that they don't raise unexpected exceptions).
You asked for a file no rule can make. Nine times in ten it is a typo, in the target or in a rule’s input:. Check spelling, check the directory, and check whether wildcards are being read correctly.
[Details on debugging wildcards.]


9.5.2 A job failed
$ snakemake --cores 1 rds/sim/n50_rho0_bayes.rds
        (command exited with non-zero exit code)
Shutting down, this might take some time.
Exiting because a job execution failed. Look below for error messages

Error in rule sim:
    message: None
    jobid: 0
    input: sim.R
    output: rds/sim/n50_rho0_bayes.rds
    shell:
        Rscript sim.R --n 50 --rho 0 --method bayes --out rds/sim/n50_rho0_bayes.rds
        (command exited with non-zero exit code)
WorkflowError:
At least one job did not complete successfully.
Snakemake reports the rule, the wildcards, and the exact shell command. Copy that command and run it yourself — you will get the R error directly, and you can step through the script interactively with the same arguments.
Two things happened that you did not see. Any output the job had already written was deleted — you get Removing output files of failed job … since they might be corrupted, so a half-written .rds can never be mistaken for a real result. (Here the script died before writing anything, so there was nothing to remove.) The log file, by contrast, was kept: if the rule declared one, the R error message is in it so it is often a good idea to start there.
The example above is the wildcard problem from Chapter 4: bayes matched {method}, so Snakemake built a perfectly good job for a method that does not exist. wildcard_constraints can turn this into a “no rule to produce” error before anything runs.


9.5.3 Incomplete files

The files below seem to be incomplete.

A previous run was stopped while a job was part-way through writing its output.
snakemake --rerun-incomplete discards the suspect files and rebuilds them.

title: 9  When things go wrong
section: 9.6 Habits that prevent most of this
text:
9.6 Habits that prevent most of this

List every script as an input. The one failure mode Snakemake cannot warn you about is the dependency you did not declare.
Dry-run before long runs. A minute may save you hours.
Then smoke-test with a small config. --config iterations=20 finds broken plumbing without simulating anything.
Give every rule a log. Debugging a parallel run without logs can be a headache.
Delete rds/ and out/ occasionally and rebuild from scratch. It is the only way to know the pipeline still works end to end — and the thing you are implicitly promising anyone who reads your paper.

title: 10  Sharing results
text:
10.1 The expensive half and the cheap half
Everything so far has assumed one machine. A coauthor who clones your repository gets the code, which is the cheap half of the project; what they do not get is the two days of compute that produced the numbers. This chapter is about handing over the expensive half, and about the one thing that goes wrong when you do.
This is where the discipline of Section 2.6 — computed results in rds/, figures and tables in out/ — stops being tidiness and starts paying rent. What you share is rds/, on its own: it is the expensive half, and a collaborator who has it can regenerate every figure and table in seconds.
A simulation that takes two days to run is not a build artifact in the way a figure is.

title: 10  Sharing results
text:
10.2 Why not git
Git is the tool you would reach for otherwise, except that git is bad at exactly this kind of content. A few hundred megabytes of .rds files bloats the repository permanently — history keeps every version you ever committed, so it is not fixed by deleting them later — diff and merge do nothing useful on serialized objects, and results derived from protected health information have no business on GitHub at all.

title: 10  Sharing results
text:
10.3 dat
dat is built for the gap the previous section described. It gives a directory a git-style push/pull workflow backed by AWS S3, without the version history:
cd rds
dat init
dat push
and, on a collaborator’s machine:
dat clone jsmith7.rds.bucket rds
dat pull
What makes it more than a wrapper around rsync is that it detects conflicts: if someone has modified a file you are about to overwrite, it says so rather than silently clobbering their work. It hashes file contents, so pushing a directory in which one of four hundred simulations changed transfers one file, and dat status will tell you whether you are in sync.
The division of labor is natural. Git holds the code: small, textual, and wanting history. dat holds the results: large, binary, and only ever wanting to be current. Each is one command to push, and a collaborator with both has your entire project.

title: 10  Sharing results
section: 10.4 What does not arrive with the files
text:
10.4 What does not arrive with the files
Sharing tool aside, there are complexities with snakemake when sharing result files.
Your coauthor clones the repository and pulls the results folder. Every .rds file is sitting there. But Snakemake’s record of how those files were made — .snakemake/, which is local and was never shared (Chapter 3):
$ snakemake -n
Job stats:
job           count
----------  -------
all               1
figure1           1
manuscript        1
sim              18
table1            1
total            22
Twenty-two jobs, eighteen of them the simulations that just arrived. On a real project that is the two days of compute the sharing was supposed to avoid.

10.4.1 Why bare --touch is not the fix
--touch marks outputs as up to date without running anything, which sounds like exactly what is needed. Run it as it comes and it does too much:
$ snakemake --touch
22 of 22 steps (100%) done
$ snakemake -n
Nothing to be done (all requested files are present and up to date).
Twenty-two of twenty-two. It asserted the figure, the table and the paper along with the simulations are up to date, and there is now nothing left for Snakemake to do. Those are precisely the things you wanted rebuilt: they cost seconds, and rebuilding them is what makes the paper on your disk yours rather than a copy of your coauthor’s.


10.4.2 The recipe: touch the results, build the rest
Be specific. Name the expensive outputs, and leave everything downstream alone:
$ snakemake --touch --force $(snakemake --summary all | awk '{print $1}' | grep '\.rds$')
18 of 18 steps (100%) done
$ snakemake -n
Job stats:
job           count
----------  -------
all               1
figure1           1
manuscript        1
table1            1
total             4
Eighteen touched, and the four jobs that matter are still to do. Then run snakemake normally and the figure, the table and the PDF are built on your machine, in seconds, from the results you were sent.
Read it inside out: --summary all prints one row per output file the workflow knows about, awk '{print $1}' takes the filename column, and grep '\.rds$' keeps the simulation results while dropping the figures, tables, PDFs and the header line. --touch acts at the jobs to be run, so --force acts on the jobs you name and nothing else.






Warning--touch is an assertion, not a check



You are telling Snakemake that files it has never seen are the correct output of the current code. It has no way to verify that, and it will believe you. If your coauthor generated those results with a different version of sim.R than the one you just cloned, the pipeline is now quietly wrong.

title: 10  Sharing results
text:
10.5 Try it
In examples/04-manuscript, with everything already built:

Delete .snakemake/ and run snakemake -n. Which of the planned jobs are the expensive ones, and which would have cost you seconds anyway?
Run bare snakemake --touch, then snakemake -n. Confirm that nothing is left to do.
Delete .snakemake/ again, run the --touch --force recipe, and then snakemake. Four jobs run. Then edit scripts/sim.R and confirm the full cascade comes back.
